question: A company runs its own application on an Azure virtual machine. Who is generally responsible for applying security updates to the virtual machine's guest operating system?

options.text: The cloud provider, because the virtual machine is hosted in Azure
The customer, because it manages the guest operating system in IaaS
The application users, because they access the service
Neither party, because the hypervisor replaces the guest operating system

explanation: In IaaS the customer manages the virtual machine's guest operating system, while the provider manages the physical hosts and underlying infrastructure.

optionExplanations.A: Hosting the VM does not transfer guest operating-system management to the provider.
optionExplanations.B: The customer manages and patches its IaaS guest operating system.
optionExplanations.C: End users are not responsible for operating-system updates merely because they use the application.
optionExplanations.D: The hypervisor hosts virtual machines; it does not replace the guest operating system.

question: A team uses an Azure infrastructure-as-a-service virtual machine. Match each responsibility to the party that generally owns it.

items.text: Secure the cloud provider's physical datacenter
Protect the customer data stored by the workload
Maintain the physical server hosting the virtual machine

explanation: The provider secures its physical datacenters and hosts; the customer remains responsible for protecting its data.

question: An attacker obtains a user's password. Which additional control is an example of a separate identity layer that can still help prevent unauthorized sign-in?

options.text: Require an additional authentication factor
Remove authorization checks from the application
Allow the password alone from any device
Publish the password to all employees

explanation: Multifactor authentication adds another identity control, so possession of a password alone need not be sufficient for sign-in.

optionExplanations.A: An additional factor can prevent a password-only sign-in.
optionExplanations.B: Removing authorization checks weakens application protection.
optionExplanations.C: Accepting the compromised password alone provides no additional identity barrier.
optionExplanations.D: Disclosing the password increases exposure instead of adding protection.

question: Match each safeguard to the defense-in-depth layer it most directly protects.

items.text: Restrict traffic between application subnets
Validate input to reduce application injection attacks
Classify and encrypt sensitive records

explanation: Segmentation protects network communications, input validation protects the application, and classification and encryption protect data.

question: A team assumes an attacker may compromise one server and limits connections from that server to other systems. Which Zero Trust principle does this most directly illustrate?

options.text: Trust the internal network by default
Eliminate all monitoring once segmentation is configured
Assume compromise and limit its potential impact
Grant permanent administrator rights to all users

explanation: Assuming compromise includes designing controls that constrain lateral movement and limit the impact of a compromised component.

optionExplanations.A: Implicit trust of internal locations conflicts with Zero Trust.
optionExplanations.B: Monitoring remains important even when segmentation is in place.
optionExplanations.C: Segmentation can reduce the blast radius if a component is compromised.
optionExplanations.D: Broad permanent privilege increases exposure and conflicts with least privilege.

question: A team needs to keep a stored file unreadable to someone who obtains the storage media without the required secret. What should the team use?

options.text: A public file name
A digest stored next to the file
An unencrypted duplicate of the file
Encryption at rest with protected key material

explanation: Encryption at rest protects the confidentiality of stored data when the decryption key is protected separately.

optionExplanations.A: A file name does not make the file contents unreadable.
optionExplanations.B: A digest can help check integrity but does not encrypt the file.
optionExplanations.C: An unencrypted copy would expose the contents to someone who obtains it.
optionExplanations.D: Encryption at rest protects stored data from readers without the appropriate key.

question: Match each cryptographic use to the concept it most directly describes.

items.text: Use the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt a large file
Encrypt data using a recipient's public key so the recipient can decrypt it with the corresponding private key
Compare a calculated digest with a trusted digest to detect a changed download

explanation: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key, asymmetric encryption uses a related key pair, and a digest comparison can detect changes to data.

question: Match each organizational activity to the governance, risk, and compliance concept it most directly represents.

items.text: Assign ownership and define policy for handling sensitive information
Assess the likelihood and impact of a possible security incident
Check practices against applicable regulatory obligations

explanation: Governance establishes direction and accountability, risk management assesses and responds to risks, and compliance concerns applicable obligations.
learningObjective: Describe Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) concepts

question: An organization passes an audit against a specific standard. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: The organization has eliminated all security risk
The audit provides evidence about the assessed scope, but other security risks can still exist
The organization no longer needs to monitor its controls
All future regulatory obligations are automatically satisfied

explanation: Compliance with an assessed standard is not the same as eliminating all security risk. Organizations should continue managing and monitoring risks and controls.

optionExplanations.A: A successful audit does not eliminate every vulnerability or risk.
optionExplanations.B: An assessment has a defined scope and does not guarantee complete security.
optionExplanations.C: Controls and risks still require ongoing monitoring.
optionExplanations.D: An audit against one scope cannot automatically satisfy all future obligations.

learningObjective: Describe Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) concepts

question: An administrator needs to manage domain users, computers, and Group Policy for an on-premises Windows network. Which directory service is designed for this environment?

options.text: Microsoft Purview Audit
Azure DDoS Protection
Active Directory Domain Services
Microsoft Sentinel

explanation: Active Directory Domain Services stores domain objects and supports on-premises administration, including Group Policy.

optionExplanations.A: Purview Audit searches activity records; it is not an on-premises directory service.
optionExplanations.B: DDoS Protection helps defend public endpoints from denial-of-service attacks.
optionExplanations.C: AD DS manages domain users and computers and supports Group Policy.
optionExplanations.D: Sentinel provides security monitoring and response, not an on-premises directory.

learningObjective: Describe the concept of directory services and Active Directory

question: For each statement about authentication and authorization, select Yes if it is accurate; otherwise select No.

items.text: Authentication verifies evidence of an identity.
A successful sign-in automatically grants every permission in an application.
Authorization can restrict a signed-in user to reading rather than editing a resource.

explanation: Authentication verifies identity; authorization separately determines which actions the identity may perform.

question: A confidential web application uses OpenID Connect to sign in a user through a trusted identity provider. Which token conveys the user's authentication information to the application?

options.text: An access token intended for a separate protected API
An authorization code before it is exchanged for tokens
A refresh token used to obtain new tokens
An ID token issued for the application

explanation: An OpenID Connect ID token contains claims about the user's authentication. A confidential client should validate the ID token; an access token is intended for a protected resource.

optionExplanations.A: An access token conveys authorization to the API, rather than user authentication information to this client.
optionExplanations.B: An authorization code is exchanged for tokens; it is not the ID token containing authentication claims.
optionExplanations.C: A refresh token obtains new tokens; it is not the ID token describing the user's authentication.
optionExplanations.D: The ID token conveys authentication information to the client application.

question: Several applications trust the same identity provider. A user signs in to the provider and can then access those applications without entering credentials again, subject to their access policies. Which identity capability does this illustrate?

options.text: Single sign-on
Encrypting a local hard disk
A network security group rule alone
Replacing authorization with a shared password

explanation: Single sign-on allows a user to sign in through an identity provider and access multiple applications that trust it, subject to application authorization and policy.

optionExplanations.A: Single sign-on lets applications reuse authentication through a trusted identity provider.
optionExplanations.B: Disk encryption protects stored data but does not establish identity-provider trust.
optionExplanations.C: A network rule controls traffic; it does not provide application sign-in.
optionExplanations.D: A shared password is not single sign-on and does not replace authorization.

question: Match each token to the purpose it most directly serves in a modern identity flow.

items.text: Give an application information about the authenticated user
Represent permission for an application to call a protected resource

explanation: An ID token conveys information about authentication to the application, while an access token is presented to an appropriate protected resource for authorization.

question: For each statement about federated identity trust, select Yes if it is accurate; otherwise select No.

items.text: Federation can allow a resource organization to accept authentication performed by another identity provider.
If organization A trusts organization B, organization B automatically trusts organization A.
Federation relies on a trust relationship between identity systems.

explanation: Federation establishes trust across identity systems. Trust in one direction does not automatically establish trust in the other direction.
